```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
#| echo: false
library(tidyverse)
library(skimr)
library(gt)

# Creating a "Netflix theme" for future table formatting
netflix_red <- "#E50914"

netflix_theme <- function(tbl) {
  tbl |>
    tab_options(heading.background.color = netflix_red,
                column_labels.background.color = "#221F1F",
                table.border.top.color = netflix_red,
                table.border.bottom.color = netflix_red) |>
    tab_style(style = cell_text(color = "white", weight = "bold"),
              locations = list(cells_title(groups = c("title", "subtitle")),
                               cells_column_labels()))
}

# Formatting for hours
fmt_hours <- scales::label_number(accuracy = 0.1,
                                  scale_cut = scales::cut_short_scale())

# Netflix formatting for ggplot charts
ggplot_theme_netflix <- function() {
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#141414", color = NA),
          panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#141414", color = NA),
          panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
          panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
          panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "#333333"),
          text = element_text(color = "white"),
          axis.text = element_text(color = "#B3B3B3"),
          plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16),
          plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "#B3B3B3"),
          plot.caption = element_text(color = "#808080", size = 8),
          legend.position = "top",
          legend.justification = "left")
}
```

{{< contents strategy-memo >}}


### 1/ Introduction

The following analysis will deep dive into Netflix's What We Watched reports, a Netflix strategic initiative to offer insights into their viewership. Based on these reports, the goal is to 1/ identify trends on content, viewership, popularity, catalog content and more and 2/ develop a strategy memo for Netflix's leadership, to inform on the 2027 original content strategy.

***What is the Netflix What We Watched Report?*** (Netflix, 2023)

- Netflix What We Watched Reports - published every 6 months starting in 2023
- The "WWW" reports aggregate total global viewership for almost the entire Netflix catalog over six-months period
- Key indicators include:

1. Hours viewed for every title - original and licensed - watched for over 50,000 hours; 
2. The premiere date for any Netflix TV series or film; and 
3. Whether a title was available globally. 

### 2/ Data Ingest and Cleaning

The very first step is to import the data and transform it to make it efficiently usable for analysis.

After importing the data:

```{r}
#| label: load-data
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#' Acquire Netflix What We Watched Reports
#' 
#' This function will acquire and standardize all data for MP#01
#' from Netflix. Because Netflix hosts the data files behind a CDN, we
#' are accessing the release pages and automatically extracting links to the
#' relevant files (with CDN hash). 
#' 
#' After import, files are stacked vertically and some basic cleaning is
#' performed. 


load_netflix_data <- function(){
  # Note to students: Make sure you have installed the tidyverse and fs packages
  #                   before beginning this assignment. If you aren't sure,
  #                   simply run `library(tidyverse)` at your R Console and, if
  #                   you don't see an error message, `tidyverse` has been 
  #                   installed. (Same for `fs`) If you still need to install
  #                   either package, use the `install.packages` function as 
  #                   demonstrated in class.
  library(tidyverse)
  library(rvest)
  library(readxl)
  library(fs)

  data_dir <- path("data", "mp01")
    
  if(!dir_exists(data_dir)){
    dir_create(data_dir, showWarnings=FALSE, recurse=TRUE)
  }
  
  NETFLIX_URLS <- list(
    `2023H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-a-netflix-engagement-report",
    `2023H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2023",
    `2024H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2024",
    `2024H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2024",
    `2025H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2025",
    `2025H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2025",
    `2026H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2026"
  )
  
  download_if_needed <- function(url, local){
    if(!file_exists(local)){
      download.file(url, local, quiet = TRUE, mode = "wb")
    }
    
    return(local)
  }
    
  NETFLIX_URLS |> 
    map(read_html) |> 
    map(html_element, xpath = "//a[contains(@href, '.xlsx')]") |> 
    map_chr(html_attr, "href") |> 
    enframe("period", "url") |> 
   mutate(path = path(data_dir, paste0(period, ".xlsx")), 
          path = map2(url, path, download_if_needed), 
          data = map(path, read_excel, skip=3, na="*"), 
          data = map(data, \(x) x |> mutate(`Release Date` = as.Date(`Release Date`)))) |>
    unnest(data) |> 
    select(-url, -path) |> 
    mutate(year=str_sub(period, 1, 4), 
           half=str_sub(period, start=6), 
           period_start = make_date(year, if_else(half==1, 1, 7), 1), 
           period_end = make_date(year, if_else(half==1, 6, 12), if_else(half==1, 30, 31))) |> 
    filter(!is.na(`Hours Viewed`)) |> 
    mutate(live_event = !is.na(Runtime) & str_detect(Runtime, "\\d+:\\d+\\*"), 
           clean_time = str_remove(Runtime, fixed("*")),
           Runtime = 60 * hour(hm(clean_time)) + minute(hm(clean_time))) |>
    select(-clean_time) |>
    mutate(Runtime = coalesce(Runtime, mean(Runtime, na.rm=TRUE)), 
           .by=Title, 
           Title = stringi::stri_trans_general(Title, "Latin-ASCII"),
           Title = str_remove(Title, " // .*"), 
           Title = str_remove(Title, "[^[:ascii:]].*"), 
           Title = str_trim(Title)) |>
    filter_out(Title == "") |>
    select(year, 
           period, 
           period_start, 
           period_end, 
           Title, 
           -half, 
           Runtime, 
           Views, 
           `Hours Viewed`, 
           `Release Date`,
           `Available Globally?`, 
           live_event) |>
    rename(title = Title,
           runtime = Runtime,
           views = Views,
           hours_viewed = `Hours Viewed`,
           release_date = `Release Date`,
           available_globally = `Available Globally?`) |>
    mutate(year = as.integer(year),
           available_globally = available_globally == "Yes") |>
    filter_out(title == "Other Shows")
}

NETFLIX_DATA <- load_netflix_data()
```
1. we rename columns in the data set to get valid `R` variable names, aligned on the same format (e.g. all lower case, multi-word separated by underscores)
2. we change variable types when appropriate, to ensure that `R` will interpret them as the correct type for future arithmetic manipulation (e.g. `year` from `chr` to `int`)
3. we filter out the "Other Shows" entries from the 2025H2 and 2026H1 reports. Netflix changed the report by aggregating many shows together under one bucket, thus not representing a single one. This would cause a distortion in title rankings and comparisons across years/periods.

### 3/ Initial Data Exploration

After an initial survey of our data, 

```{r}
#| label: eda-glimpse
#| code-fold: false
glimpse(NETFLIX_DATA)
```

we note that the data is a mix of numeric, categorical, date, and logical variables. It's composed of **`r scales::comma(nrow(NETFLIX_DATA))`** rows and **`r ncol(NETFLIX_DATA)`** columns.

We also note that some columns like `views` appear to contain `NA` values, potentially limiting the analyses that rely on this column.

Finally, we can get an idea of what one row represents: one title in one period. It's worth noting that titles can repeat across periods.

We now take another look at the data, focusing now more on the statistical information,

```{r}
#| label: eda-skim
#| code-fold: false
skim(NETFLIX_DATA)
```

we see that the data set is complete for the majority of the variables, except for numeric `runtime` (**`r scales::percent(mean(!is.na(NETFLIX_DATA$runtime)), accuracy = 1)`**) and `views` (**`r scales::percent(mean(!is.na(NETFLIX_DATA$views)), accuracy = 1)`**) where the `complete_rate` is below 80%. `release_date` has a complete rate of **`r scales::percent(mean(!is.na(NETFLIX_DATA$release_date)), accuracy = 1)`**, worth noting for further analysis (e.g. analyzing viewership based on release date will be limited).

The mean for `hours_viewed` is **`r fmt_hours(mean(NETFLIX_DATA$hours_viewed))`** and the median is **`r fmt_hours(median(NETFLIX_DATA$hours_viewed))`**, where the mean is about **`r round(mean(NETFLIX_DATA$hours_viewed) / median(NETFLIX_DATA$hours_viewed), 1)`**x the median. We note a heavily skewed distribution, indicating that some titles may be very popular compared to others.


*Note:* we include a table to see which top titles in what period could explain the skewed distribution. 

```{r}
#| label: eda-gt-top5
NETFLIX_DATA |>
  slice_max(hours_viewed, n = 5) |>
  select(title, period, hours_viewed) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = "The 5 Netflix Titles with the Most Hours Viewed",
             subtitle = "The biggest hits in Netflix's WWW reports, starting 2023") |>
  cols_label(title = "Title",
             period = "Period",
             hours_viewed = "Hours Viewed") |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(hours_viewed),
             suffixing = TRUE, decimals = 1) |>
  tab_source_note("Source: Netflix - What We Watched reports, 2023H1-2026H1") |>
  netflix_theme()
```

The most popular titles are seasons from different shows, indicating that the popularity is broken down by season, and not show overall.

### 4/ Exploratory Questions

Now that we have looked at the data set structure and gotten an idea of its content, we deep dive into some key representative facts about the WWW reports. This allows us to understand the specific content, and not only the statistical components.


```{r}
#| label: t5-calculations
#| code-summary: "Show calculations"

# Q1
date_start <- min(NETFLIX_DATA$period_start)
date_end <- max(NETFLIX_DATA$period_end)

# Q2
n_titles <- n_distinct(NETFLIX_DATA$title)

# Q3
bridgerton_hours <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(str_detect(title, "Bridgerton")) |>
  summarize(total = sum(hours_viewed)) |>
  pull(total)

# Q4
stranger_things_hours <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(str_detect(title, "Stranger Things")) |>
  filter_out(str_detect(title, "Beyond")) |>
  filter_out(str_detect(title, "Tales")) |>
  filter_out(str_detect(title, "Fireplace")) |>
  summarize(total = sum(hours_viewed)) |>
  pull(total)

# Q5
top10_share <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(period == "2026H1") |>
  arrange(desc(hours_viewed)) |>
  summarize(share = sum(hours_viewed[1:10]) / sum(hours_viewed)) |>
  pull(share)

# Q6
available_globally_by_title <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  summarize(global = any(available_globally), .by = title) |>
  summarize(share = mean(global)) |>
  pull(share)

available_globally_by_hours <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  summarize(share = sum(hours_viewed[available_globally], na.rm = TRUE) /
                    sum(hours_viewed[!is.na(available_globally)])) |>
  pull(share)
```

First, we note that the date ranges from **`r format(date_start, "%B %d, %Y")`** to **`r format(date_end, "%B %d, %Y")`**. The reports thus started in 2023, and are broken down into **`r round(lubridate::interval(min(NETFLIX_DATA$period_start), min(NETFLIX_DATA$period_end)) / months(1))`**-month periods (with **`r n_distinct(NETFLIX_DATA$period)`** total periods so far).

Besides the total number of entries in the data set, what is interesting is to see how many distinct titles exist. The total number of shows and movies in the data set is **`r scales::comma(n_titles)`**. This is very different from the number of entries, **`r scales::comma(nrow(NETFLIX_DATA))`**, confirming that titles may appear several times across periods.

Out of the very popular shows on Netflix, we take a look at the Bridgerton Universe and Stranger Things. While the Bridgerton Universe is broadly viewed with **`r fmt_hours(bridgerton_hours)`** total hours, the five seasons of the Stranger Things show accumulate **`r fmt_hours(stranger_things_hours)`** total hours. It surpasses the Bridgerton Universe by **`r scales::percent(stranger_things_hours / bridgerton_hours - 1, accuracy = 1)`** (a close race).

Another exploration is to see what percentage of the total watch time in the first 6 months of 2026 (2026H1) was spent on the top 10 titles. For 2026H1, **`r scales::percent(top10_share, accuracy = 0.1)`** of watch time was spent on the top 10 titles, out of all **`r scales::comma(sum(NETFLIX_DATA$period == "2026H1"))`** available titles. 

Finally, to get a sense of Netflix's global reach, we look at what fraction of the catalog is available globally by both title and hours viewed. The share of the Netflix catalog available globally is **`r scales::percent(available_globally_by_title, accuracy = 0.1)`** by title, and **`r scales::percent(available_globally_by_hours, accuracy = 0.1)`** weighted by hours viewed. This demonstrates that shows available globally are more popular in terms of viewership, even if they are not as offered as regional content, compared to the whole catalog. 

### 5/ Exploratory Tables

Now we dig deeper into the analysis, by looking at specific aspects of the data set, to compare, evaluate and draw preliminary conclusions. Tables are used to help to visualize the outputs.

The goal is to retrieve the top title (by total hours viewed) in each period, and compare it to total viewership. This helps answer the question: how dominant can a single hit be?

```{r}
#| label: t6-q1-top-title
top_by_period <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  mutate(share = hours_viewed / sum(hours_viewed), .by = period) |>
  slice_max(hours_viewed, n = 1, by = period, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  select(period, title, hours_viewed, share)

top_by_period |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = "Top Title per Period",
             subtitle = "TV shows dominate movies in top titles across each period") |>
  cols_label(period = "Period",
             title = "Title",
             hours_viewed = "Hours Viewed",
             share = "Share of Period Hours Viewed") |>
  fmt_number(columns = hours_viewed, suffixing = TRUE, decimals = 1) |>
  fmt_percent(columns = share, decimals = 1) |>
  tab_source_note("Source: Netflix - What We Watched reports, 2023H1-2026H1") |>
  netflix_theme()
```

Across periods, similar trends are observed: hours viewed range from **`r fmt_hours(min(top_by_period$hours_viewed))`** to **`r fmt_hours(max(top_by_period$hours_viewed))`**, and the share is stable and similar across periods, from **`r scales::percent(min(top_by_period$share), accuracy = 0.1)`** to **`r scales::percent(max(top_by_period$share), accuracy = 0.1)`**. This suggests that, although the top title by hours viewed can be much higher than other shows, the share is relatively small (meaning that the viewership is either spread out across the catalog, or that the catalog choice is very extensive).

Furthermore, as observed in the table, the top titles are TV shows across all periods. This indicates the biggest hits on the platform are recurring popular TV shows (with Bridgerton and Squid Game appearing twice, different seasons).

Now that the top titles have been reviewed, we assess the evolution of available titles and run time across the whole catalog *(2023H1-2026H1)*. Although limited since the reports started in 2023, it matters to see how Netflix evolved across the years and if it impacted the run times. 

```{r}
#| label: t6-q2-catalog-size

missing_by_period <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  summarize(missing_runtime = mean(is.na(runtime)),
            .by = period)

catalog_by_period <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  summarize(n_titles = n_distinct(title),
            total_runtime_minutes = sum(runtime, na.rm = TRUE),
            total_runtime_hours = total_runtime_minutes / 60,
            .by = period)

catalog_by_period |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = "Netflix's Catalog Evolution Across Periods",
             subtitle = "A steady growth across the catalog, despite a drop in number of titles between 2023H1 and H2") |>
  cols_label(period = "Period",
             n_titles = "Number of Titles",
             total_runtime_minutes = md("Total Run Time (*minutes*)"),
             total_runtime_hours = md("Equivalent Total Run Time (*hours*)")) |>
  fmt_number(columns = n_titles, decimals = 0) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(total_runtime_minutes, total_runtime_hours), suffixing = TRUE, decimals = 1) |>
  tab_footnote(footnote = "Large amount of missing values in the run time of the 2023H1 period.",
               locations = cells_body(columns = c(total_runtime_minutes,
                                                  total_runtime_hours),
                                      rows = period == "2023H1")) |>
  tab_source_note("Source: Netflix - What We Watched reports, 2023H1-2026H1") |>
  netflix_theme()
```
2023H1 shows a high number of titles available, with a low total run time value (comparatively to other periods). We note a steep decline in number of titles (by **`r scales::percent(1 - catalog_by_period$n_titles[catalog_by_period$period == "2023H2"] / catalog_by_period$n_titles[catalog_by_period$period == "2023H1"], accuracy = 1)`**) between 2023H1 and 2023H2. We run a check on missing run time in 2023H1 compared to all other periods. The fraction of missing values reaches **`r scales::percent(missing_by_period$missing_runtime[missing_by_period$period == "2023H1"], accuracy = 1)`** for 2023H1, compared to all other periods with at most **`r scales::percent(max(missing_by_period$missing_runtime[missing_by_period$period != "2023H1"]), accuracy = 0.1)`**. Netflix made improvements in the reports with the May 2024 update, by adding run time and views. This confirms that the first report, 2023H1 was published without these columns, thus explaining the low run time (Netflix, 2023). 

Despite the decline, a steady growth appears in the following periods, without any decline across both number of titles and total run time.

*Note:* titles with less than 50,000 hours of watch time are omitted. Some titles may therefore be missing ( as stated in Netflix, 2023).

Since the reports started, we wonder which titles have the most ***consistent*** high viewership across all periods. This question is particularly interesting, as the titles that will show may likely be ‘staples’, that viewers fall back on over and over. They will likely be present in every period (given that the show was already out starting 2023H1). 

```{r}
#| label: t6-q3-highest-viewership
n_periods_total <- n_distinct(NETFLIX_DATA$period)

staples <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  summarize(n_periods = n_distinct(period),
            avg_hours = mean(hours_viewed),
            min_hours = min(hours_viewed),
            sd_hours = sd(hours_viewed),
            .by = title) |>
  filter(n_periods == n_periods_total) |>
  mutate(cv = sd_hours / avg_hours) |>
  slice_max(min_hours, n = 10) |>
  select(title, avg_hours, min_hours, cv)

staples |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = "Highest Consistent Viewership Across all Periods",
             subtitle = md("Consistently high viewership around *old* shows, with high variability around season outings and revivals")) |>
  cols_label(title = "Title",
             avg_hours = "Avg. Hours Viewed per Period",
             min_hours = "Lowest Period",
             cv = md("Variability (*CV*)")) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(avg_hours, min_hours), suffixing = TRUE, decimals = 1) |>
  fmt_percent(columns = cv, decimals = 0) |>
  tab_source_note("Note 1: Titles present across all periods, ranked by lowest period hours.") |>
  tab_source_note("Note 2: CV = standard deviation / mean.") |>
  tab_source_note("Source: Netflix - What We Watched reports, 2023H1-2026H1") |>
  netflix_theme()
```
This output suggests that, across all periods, the most reliable titles with the consistent highest viewership are mostly licensed classics, with one Original exception. 

We note two different kinds in this table: **`r sum(staples$cv < 0.3)`** shows with rather low variability with 30% as a threshold (between **`r scales::percent(min(staples$cv[staples$cv < 0.3]), accuracy = 1)`** and **`r scales::percent(max(staples$cv[staples$cv < 0.3]), accuracy = 1)`**), and **`r sum(staples$cv >= 0.3)`** shows with high variability (between **`r scales::percent(min(staples$cv[staples$cv >= 0.3]), accuracy = 1)`** and **`r scales::percent(max(staples$cv[staples$cv >= 0.3]), accuracy = 1)`**). Looking at the titles and with common knowledge, we note a potential explanation around new season releases or digital revival, increasing viewership. 

Indeed, when shows have new releases, or digital revivals, it can be assumed that, although viewership is present, the spikes raise their average and variability. The biggest hits center more around new shows, while the most consistent ones are more "older" shows.

What about the share of shows vs. movies? The raw data set doesn't give that indication. To find the answer, we define two criteria that will be used for the output:

1. Length: anything over ~4 hours is almost certainly a TV show, not a movie
2. “Season”: if a title has “Season” or "Limited Series" in it, it is almost certainly a TV show

It is important to note that:

1. As previously found, there is a high number of missing values in the run time (especially for 2023H1). We therefore use a criterion to classify titles with missing run time with the keywords only
2. The way Netflix names titles is a bit inconsistent in how it represents different seasons of TV shows (e.g. Seinfeld: Season 1 and Seinfeld: Season 3, but Stranger Things and Stranger Things 3). The ratios may therefore be limited, if the classification is solely based on title names

```{r}
#| label: t6-q4-shows-movies
shows_movies <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  mutate(type = if_else(str_detect(title, "Season|Limited Series") |
                          coalesce(runtime > 240, FALSE),
                        "Shows", "Movies")) |>
  summarize(hours = sum(hours_viewed), .by = c(period, type)) |>
  mutate(share = hours / sum(hours), .by = period) |>
  select(period, type, share) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = type, values_from = share)

shows_movies |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = "Fraction of Viewership Classified by Shows and Movies",
             subtitle = "Overall stable distribution between shows and movies, with shows leading in the race") |>
  cols_label(period = "Period") |>
  fmt_percent(columns = c(Shows, Movies), decimals = 1) |>
  tab_footnote("Note: TV show/movie classified based on title keywords and run time over 4 hours.") |>
  tab_footnote(footnote = "High number of run time values missing in 2023H1, classification based on title keywords only.",
               locations = cells_body(columns = c(Shows, Movies),
                                      rows = period == "2023H1")) |>
  tab_source_note("Source: Netflix - What We Watched reports, 2023H1-2026H1") |>
  netflix_theme()
```
We note a common pattern across all periods, with an average of **`r scales::percent(mean(shows_movies$Shows[shows_movies$period != "2023H1"]), accuracy = 0.1)`** viewing time for shows and **`r scales::percent(mean(shows_movies$Movies[shows_movies$period != "2023H1"]), accuracy = 0.1)`** for movies. We exclude 2023H1 from these averages for the same reason mentioned above, the **`r scales::percent(missing_by_period$missing_runtime[missing_by_period$period == "2023H1"], accuracy = 1)`** missing run time. 

Based on the rule, titles with missing run times are classified based solely on the presence of keywords such as "season". This may expose an issue in the ratio shows vs. movies in 2023H1 versus all other periods.

Furthermore, we note that there is a specific variable, which flags a given title as a `live_event` or not. Live Events are programs that stream live on Netflix. It's a specific format, an innovative strategy for Netflix (who traditionally runs pre-recorded content), varying from sports events to comedy specials.

*Note*: viewership will almost certainly be lower for Live Events, as it's short "one-shot" content. Therefore, the analysis cannot purely compare hours_viewed in order to get a real sense of popularity by viewership.

```{r}
#| label: t6-q5-live-events
runtime_by_group <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  distinct(title, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  mutate(group = case_when(
    live_event ~ "Live Events",
    str_detect(title, "Season|Limited Series") |
      coalesce(runtime > 240, FALSE) ~ "Shows",
    TRUE ~ "Movies")) |>
  summarize(median_runtime_hours = median(runtime, na.rm = TRUE) / 60,
            .by = group)

live_vs_taped <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  summarize(hours = sum(hours_viewed),
            live = any(live_event),
            .by = title) |>
  mutate(type = if_else(live, "Live Events", "Pre-taped")) |>
  summarize(n_titles = n(),
            avg_hours = mean(hours),
            median_hours = median(hours),
            top10_avg_hours = mean(head(sort(hours, decreasing = TRUE), 10)),
            .by = type)

live_vs_taped |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = "Comparison of Pre-taped and Live Events Content Viewership",
             subtitle = "Although Pre-taped performs higher in hours viewed, Live Events can create value in high 'one-shot' viewership") |>
  cols_label(type = "Content Category",
             n_titles = "Titles",
             avg_hours = "Avg. Hours Viewed",
             median_hours = "Median Hours Viewed",
             top10_avg_hours = "Top 10 Avg. Hours Viewed") |>
  fmt_number(columns = n_titles, decimals = 0) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(avg_hours, median_hours, top10_avg_hours),
             suffixing = TRUE, decimals = 1) |>
  tab_source_note("Note 1: Hours are summed per title across all periods.") |>
  tab_source_note("Note 2: Top 10 Avg. represents the average hours of the 10 titles with highest hours viewed in each group.") |>
  tab_source_note("Source: Netflix - What We Watched reports, 2023H1-2026H1") |>
  netflix_theme()
```

The number of distinct titles for each category confirms that, traditionally, Netflix runs more Pre-taped content than Live Events (**`r scales::comma(live_vs_taped$n_titles[live_vs_taped$type == "Pre-taped"])`** vs. **`r scales::comma(live_vs_taped$n_titles[live_vs_taped$type == "Live Events"])`**).

However, when we look at the median hours viewed, which isn't affected by outliers (e.g. big hits in Pre-taped content), we see that it's almost identical across both (**`r fmt_hours(live_vs_taped$median_hours[live_vs_taped$type == "Pre-taped"])`** for Pre-taped and **`r fmt_hours(live_vs_taped$median_hours[live_vs_taped$type == "Live Events"])`** for Live Events). This indicates that the typical titles for each category perform similarly, even though hours viewed averages are very different (**`r fmt_hours(live_vs_taped$avg_hours[live_vs_taped$type == "Pre-taped"])`** vs. **`r fmt_hours(live_vs_taped$avg_hours[live_vs_taped$type == "Live Events"])`**).

Finally, we analyze "top tiers" with a top 10 viewership metric for each category, and we notice a big gap between a **`r fmt_hours(live_vs_taped$top10_avg_hours[live_vs_taped$type == "Pre-taped"])`** average hours for Pre-taped content and **`r fmt_hours(live_vs_taped$top10_avg_hours[live_vs_taped$type == "Live Events"])`** for Live Events. That is **`r round(live_vs_taped$top10_avg_hours[live_vs_taped$type == "Pre-taped"] / live_vs_taped$top10_avg_hours[live_vs_taped$type == "Live Events"])`**x more.

A few plausible explanations include:

1. The popularity of Pre-taped content outshines Live Events in terms of lifetime. TV shows have been running and are being watched for a long time, thus surpassing Live Events which are more punctual and recent
2. The median length of a TV show (being the dominating type in Netflix's catalog, as noted before) is much longer than a one-shot Live Event (with **`r round(runtime_by_group$median_runtime_hours[runtime_by_group$group == "Shows"], 1)`** hours for TV shows and **`r round(runtime_by_group$median_runtime_hours[runtime_by_group$group == "Live Events"], 1)`** hours for Live Events). Even if median hours viewed are almost identical, a TV show will almost always count for more hours viewed.

Both types create value in a different way. Pre-taped content will shine on the long run, with more viewership across the years (and spikes with hits), whereas "one-shot" Live Events do create value by building a high audience in one moment (which can bring a lot of adjacent revenues such as advertising, sponsorship etc.).

::: {#strategy-memo style="border-left: 6px solid #E50914; background-color: #F7F7F7; padding: 1.5em; border-radius: 6px; margin-bottom: 3em;"}

2. Context

```{r}
#| label: memo-growth-calculation
#| echo: false
hours_by_period <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter_out(period == "2023H1") |>
  summarize(total_hours = sum(hours_viewed), .by = period) |>
  arrange(period)
```

Given the preparation fo the 2027 budget, the What We Watched Reports (2023H1-2026H1) was used to analyze past trends on key metrics (hours viewed, availability globally and content typology). Overall, the Netflix viewership has increased over the periods since the reports started, with a **`r scales::percent(last(hours_by_period$total_hours) / first(hours_by_period$total_hours) - 1, accuracy = 1)`** growth, as noted in the graph below. The goal is to find the right strategy to increase viewership on a long-term basis.

*Note*: 2023H1 omitted from data, different scope.

```{r}

  geom_text(aes(label = fmt_hours(total_hours)),
            vjust = -1, color = "white", size = 3.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = fmt_hours,
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.15))) +
  labs(title = "Netflix Content Viewership starting 2023H2",
       subtitle = "Continuous growth over the years",
       x = NULL, y = "Total Hours Viewed",
       caption = "Excluded from the analysis: 'Other Shows' entries.\n2023H1 omitted from the data due to a different scope, udpated starting 2023H2.\nSource: Netflix - What We Watched reports, 2023H1-2026H1") +
  ggplot_theme_netflix()
```

2. Global originals + licensed base (global vs. licensed): 24.6% of titles → 52.1% of viewing; staples are mostly licensed

Our research has found that, although regional content is more widespread (with XX% of total hours viewed), globally available titles (with XX% of total hours viewed) absorb XX% of total viewership. This indicates that the global availability (mainly composed of Netflix Originals), are more efficient. bla bla bla

Focusing on developing XXX

```{r}
#| label: memo-chart-1
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "75%"
#| fig-align: "center"
#| fig-height: 4
global_chart <- tibble(
  measure = factor(rep(c("Share of Titles", "Share of Hours Viewed"), each = 2),
                   levels = c("Share of Titles", "Share of Hours Viewed")),
  availability = rep(c("Global", "Regional"), times = 2),
  share = c(available_globally_by_title, 1 - available_globally_by_title,
            available_globally_by_hours, 1 - available_globally_by_hours)
)

ggplot(global_chart, aes(x = measure, y = share, fill = availability)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +

            position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5),
            color = "white", fontface = "bold", size = 5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Global" = netflix_red, "Regional" = "#564D4D")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(title = "[TITLE TO DO]",
       subtitle = "[KEY TAKEWAY TO DO]",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = NULL,

  ggplot_theme_netflix()
```

3. Live events as a complement (big hits vs. long tail): typical live ≈ typical pre-taped; no blockbusters; value through simultaneous audiences

A typical title performs as well for both category, with XXM vs XXM. However, the average hours viewed is longer for pre-taped (logic since it's longer run time + historically longest in Netflix's history). 

Strategy: increase "one-shot" Live events to bring punctual value and increase revenue around advertising, sponsorship etc.

```{r}
#| label: memo-chart-2
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "75%"
#| fig-align: "center"
live_chart <- live_vs_taped |>
  select(type, median_hours, avg_hours, top10_avg_hours) |>
  pivot_longer(-type, names_to = "metric", values_to = "hours") |>
  mutate(metric = factor(metric,
                         levels = c("median_hours", "avg_hours", "top10_avg_hours"),
                         labels = c("Typical Title\n(median)",
                                    "Average Title",
                                    "Top 10 Titles\n(average)")))

ggplot(live_chart, aes(x = metric, y = hours, fill = type)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.7), width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = fmt_hours(hours)),
            position = position_dodge(width = 0.7),
            vjust = -0.4, color = "white", size = 3.5) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = fmt_hours) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Live Events" = netflix_red,
                               "Pre-taped" = "#564D4D")) +
  labs(title = "[TITLE TO DO]",
       subtitle = "[KEY TAKEAWAY TO DO]",
       x = NULL, y = "Hours viewed per title (log scale)", fill = NULL,
       caption = "Hours are summed per title across all periods. Source: Netflix - What We Watched reports, 2023H1-2026H1") +
  ggplot_theme_netflix()
```

4. Limitations (hours favor long content; 2023H1 gaps, revenues streams missing)

Basing recommendations solely on hours can bias the results, as viewership varies largely based on typology of content (movies vs. TV shows vs. one shot Live Events). Furthermore, the run time data for 2023H1 is widely missing, causing a potential bias in Period over Period PoP trend analysis.

The hours viewed alone for a given title doesn't measure its success (Netflix, 2023). The reports are not compared against any revenue streams (income vs. spent), making it hard to propose solid recommendations by analyzing the viewership vs. associated costs. Finally, a part of non-English titles was dropped in this analysis (noting that all non-English titles accounted for 30% of viewership in the first published report 2023H1) (Netflix, 2023).
